question.text: Saraswati Growth Partners (Cat II AIF) is deciding between a Series C cheque into a profitable SaaS company and a Pre-Series A cheque into a pre-profit fintech. Per Chapter 9, which characterisation is CORRECT about the two strategies the fund would be executing?

answer.text: Both are Venture Capital strategies since both are in the VC-to-PE continuum.
Series C is primarily Venture Capital (first institutional round); Pre-Series A is Private Equity.
Series C is Private Equity / later-stage scaling capital; Pre-Series A is early-stage Venture Capital — PE focuses on scaling mature businesses, VC on early-stage unlisted growth companies.
Both are Angel investments since both companies are unlisted.

explanation.text: The Logic: Chapter 9 draws a clear line: Private Equity invests in 'mature businesses … established business model … scaled up for further growth' — Series C onwards. Venture Capital is the 'first stage of institutional financing' post-angel — Pre-Series A / Series A / B. So the SaaS Series C cheque is a PE strategy, while the Pre-Series A fintech cheque is a VC strategy. The Trap: Option A ignores the VC/PE boundary Chapter 9 explicitly draws. Option B inverts the mapping — Series A is the 'first round of venture capital' per the chapter, not PE. Option D confuses any unlisted investment with 'angel' — angels are strictly Stage 1-2 HNI capital. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C (All-Cat Manager — now superseded for the Cat I/II track) tested this VC/PE boundary. XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) is listed-only and never touches this mapping. XIX-E (Cat III) is irrelevant — Cat III typically uses listed-market hedge strategies, not stage-based classification. Manager's Pro-Tip: When writing the PPM strategy section, avoid calling your fund a 'VC + PE' blended vehicle — LPs then benchmark you against the harder of the two IRR peer groups. Pick a dominant lane (say 70% Series B/C) and position the other sleeve as 'opportunistic'.
